name: quickjs-jit (Longbridge JIT-enabled QuickJS-NG distribution)
language: Rust (with the vendored QuickJS-NG C engine)
baseline: QuickJS-NG interpreter (same runtime with the JIT detached); Bun 1.4.0 (JavaScriptCore) also measured as the external target
workload: 35 JavaScript scenarios (scalar loops, fibonacci, calls, property access, typed arrays, JSON, regexp, collections, exceptions); latency in ms per ten workload calls, median over processes of each process's upper-median of 16 timed batches, paired geometric-mean ratios with 95% confidence intervals.
claimed_speedup: Complete 35-scenario Linux x86_64 matrix measured 2026-09-30 (README): versus same-version QuickJS 23 scenarios faster, 7 tied, 5 slower; e.g. scalar-control-flow 49.2x faster (2.13 ms vs 0.0434 ms), scalar-expressions 47.4x, quickjs-bitops 42.6x, fibonacci-iterative 45.8x, fibonacci-recursive 27.1x (9.91 ms vs 0.361 ms), float64-dense 22.2x; slower cases collections 0.98x, strings-json 0.96x, json-codec 0.96x, map-set-bigint 0.99x, exceptions-promises-async 0.98x. Versus Bun 1.4.0 all 35 scenarios are slower (closest fibonacci-recursive 0.73x of Bun speed, widest methods-dynamic 0.012x).
compiler_and_flags: rustc 1.98.1 / LLVM 22.1.8, release build; QuickJS-NG commit fd0a0210b7be00957751871e7e01b8291268fc29 is the interpreter control; Bun 1.4.0 default flags; the C engine's own optimisation flags are not stated in the README
hardware: 13th Gen Intel Core i7-13700KF, Linux 7.2.5 x86_64, CPU 8 pinned, powersave governor (the same README also has an Apple M3 matrix, no CPU pinning)
stars_or_usage: 15 stars; published as the quickjs-jit crate (rquickjs fork)
tradeoffs: Experimental tiered JIT on top of QuickJS-NG; the JIT ABI depends on internal QuickJS structure layouts so the runtime, core and sys crates must be the same patch version; consumed as a Rust crate (rquickjs API), so C++ users would have to take the C engine plus JIT sources from the repo directly.
caveats: First-party matrix; the benchmarks/ directory exists in the repo but I only read the README tables. Not a V8 win: every scenario is slower than Bun (JavaScriptCore) and V8 was not measured. Wins are on scalar and numeric kernels (many 20-50x); string, JSON, collection and exception scenarios are tied or about 1-4% slower than the interpreter, and the README documents a 0.12.10 regression fixed in 0.12.11. The implementation is mostly Rust, so it falls outside a strict C++ filter; the repository metadata shows AI-assisted development (AGENTS.md, commit co-author).
found_via: WebSearch (github.com/gitlab.com only): JavaScript engine in C or C++ "faster than QuickJS" OR "faster than V8" interpreter benchmark README -> longbridge/quickjs-jit pull request #30; README opened via raw.githubusercontent.com and github.com

name: Pythran
baseline: CPython (interpreted Python; version inferred 3.12 for the dev-branch table, tables also exist for 3.10, 3.11, 3.13 and 3.14)
workload: 13 numeric kernels (Ackermann, Bellman-Ford, Dijkstra, Euler, midpoint explicit/fixed, RK4, four finite-difference solvers, molecular dynamics, splines); execution time in ms, compilation excluded.
claimed_speedup: pyccel-benchmarks dev-branch execution-time table (ms, CPython column vs pythran_gnu column): Ackermann 456.00 vs 2.70; Bellman Ford 1950.00 vs 4.58; Dijkstra 5530.00 vs 18.00; Euler 3900.00 vs 26.10; RK4 19800.00 vs 152.00; FD L Convection 2280.00 vs 1.52; FD Poisson 6140.00 vs 2.93; FD Laplace 729.00 vs 67.10; M-D 8530.00 vs 36.30. Ratios across the 12 supported kernels range from 10.9x (FD Laplace) to 2095.6x (FD Poisson), geometric mean about 264x (derived from page data). Splines is unsupported ('-').
compiler_and_flags: pythran_gnu configuration: the default pythran config plus -O3 -march=native -mtune=native -mavx -ffast-math (GNU compiler family, version not stated); an Intel-compiler variant (pythran_intel) is also reported
stars_or_usage: 2.1k stars; on PyPI (0.19.0 per the PyPI JSON API); Debian, Arch and Fedora packages per the README
tradeoffs: Only a numeric subset of Python (with NumPy support) compiles; needs '# pythran export' signatures and a C++ compiler at build time; produces a native extension module with the same interface.
caveats: Numbers come from the README of the Pyccel developers' benchmark repository (pyccel/pyccel-benchmarks), not from the project's own repo; CPU model, OS, GNU compiler version and Intel compiler version are not stated; the 'dev branch' table is dated 'Mon Aug 3 10:56:24 UTC 2026' and its Python version (3.12) is inferred from the result image file name devel_performance_312_execution.svg. Execution times exclude compilation (the README compile-time table, unit not labelled and presumably seconds, lists 0.33 to 8.31 per kernel across all tools). The CPython column is plain interpreted Python on scalar-loop style numeric kernels adapted from Burkardt and Barba examples (per the README; I did not open the kernel sources), so the large ratios do not transfer to code that already runs in NumPy. Evidence is a third-party shootout run by the Pyccel developers (a competitor of Pythran), which is why it is tier B rather than A; the Pythran repo's own README carries no benchmark numbers. -ffast-math is enabled for the Pythran column.
found_via: WebSearch: pythran vs CPython speedup benchmark C++ Python compiler numba pyccel comparison; PyPI JSON API (pypi.org/pypi/pythran/json) opened; numbers from github.com/pyccel/pyccel-benchmarks README

workload: 13 numeric kernels (Ackermann, Bellman-Ford, Dijkstra, Euler, midpoint explicit/fixed, RK4, four finite-difference solvers, molecular dynamics, splines); execution time in ms, compilation excluded.

caveats: Numbers come from the README of the Pyccel developers' benchmark repository (pyccel/pyccel-benchmarks), not from the project's own repo; CPU model, OS, GNU compiler version and Intel compiler version are not stated; the 'dev branch' table is dated 'Mon Aug 3 10:56:24 UTC 2026' and its Python version (3.12) is inferred from the result image file name devel_performance_312_execution.svg. Execution times exclude compilation (the README compile-time table, unit not labelled and presumably seconds, lists 0.33 to 8.31 per kernel across all tools). The CPython column is plain interpreted Python on scalar-loop style numeric kernels adapted from Burkardt and Barba examples (per the README; I did not open the kernel sources), so the large ratios do not transfer to code that already runs in NumPy. Numba is the weakest of the three accelerators on FD Laplace (1.4x) and on the finite-difference kernels where Pythran is 5-10x faster; third-party shootout run by the Pyccel developers, so tier B. name: Pyccel
language: Python (transpiler that emits Fortran or C)
baseline: CPython (interpreted Python; version inferred 3.12 for the dev-branch table, tables also exist for 3.10, 3.11, 3.13 and 3.14)
workload: 13 numeric kernels (Ackermann, Bellman-Ford, Dijkstra, Euler, midpoint explicit/fixed, RK4, four finite-difference solvers, molecular dynamics, splines); execution time in ms, compilation excluded.
claimed_speedup: pyccel-benchmarks dev-branch execution-time table (ms, CPython column vs pyccel_gnu_c column; the Fortran backend is reported too): Ackermann 456.00 vs 1.33 (Fortran 1.28); Bellman Ford 1950.00 vs 3.28; Euler 3900.00 vs 6.94; Midpoint Fixed 40000.00 vs 47.40; RK4 19800.00 vs 57.00; FD Poisson 6140.00 vs 3.78; FD Laplace 729.00 vs 151.00; M-D 8530.00 vs 74.50; Splines 1770.00 vs 13.30. Ratios across the 13 kernels range from 4.8x (FD Laplace) to 1624.3x (FD Poisson), geometric mean about 336x for the GNU C backend (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: pyccel_gnu_c / pyccel_gnu_fortran configurations with -O3 -march=native -mtune=native -mavx -ffast-math (GNU compiler family, version not stated); Intel-compiler variants also reported
stars_or_usage: 398 stars; on PyPI (2.2.3 per the PyPI JSON API); JOSS 2023 paper (Pyccel: a Python-to-X transpiler for scientific high-performance computing) cited in the README
tradeoffs: Restricted, statically typed Python subset; emits readable C or Fortran that is compiled and wrapped as a Python extension; supports NumPy and SciPy calls through generated code.
caveats: Numbers come from the README of the Pyccel developers' benchmark repository (pyccel/pyccel-benchmarks), not from the project's own repo; CPU model, OS, GNU compiler version and Intel compiler version are not stated; the 'dev branch' table is dated 'Mon Aug 3 10:56:24 UTC 2026' and its Python version (3.12) is inferred from the result image file name devel_performance_312_execution.svg. Execution times exclude compilation (the README compile-time table, unit not labelled and presumably seconds, lists 0.33 to 8.31 per kernel across all tools). The CPython column is plain interpreted Python on scalar-loop style numeric kernels adapted from Burkardt and Barba examples (per the README; I did not open the kernel sources), so the large ratios do not transfer to code that already runs in NumPy. First-party benchmark (the Pyccel team's own repository), hence tier C even though the code, flags and Python versions are public. Pyccel is slower than Pythran on Dijkstra, M-D and FD Laplace in the same table. The JOSS paper was not opened (host blocked), so no peer-reviewed numbers are used.
found_via: WebSearch: pythran vs CPython speedup benchmark C++ Python compiler numba pyccel comparison (JOSS paper hit) -> github.com/pyccel/pyccel and pyccel-benchmarks; PyPI JSON API opened

name: cpy
workload: README 'How fast' section: a numeric loop, building a list, filling and reading a dict, a hot attribute-access loop, and a recursive fib(30), run as the scripts in tests/ on one machine.
claimed_speedup: '1.2x-50x faster than CPython' on the numeric loop, list building, dict fill/read and attribute-access benchmarks; the call-heavy recursive fib(30) benchmark is 'about on par' (README, no per-benchmark times given).
hardware: 'single-machine numbers' (CPU not stated); README says it is built to be developed and run on a phone (Termux) as well as PC or server
stars_or_usage: 0 stars at the time of the check
tradeoffs: Python subset: 64-bit int only (overflow raises OverflowError), no bytes/bytearray, complex numbers, match, async/await, __slots__ or metaclasses beyond type(...); standard library limited to a few built-in modules; no JIT (README says it will not out-run PyPy).
caveats: Brand-new repository (the six visible commits are all dated 2026-09-22). README gives a range with no per-benchmark numbers, no compiler or flags and no CPU; tests/compare_python.sh only diffs program output against CPython (I read it), so there is no timing script to reproduce the ratios. Tests are 'verified against CPython 3.12' for output, not speed. Low confidence.
found_via: WebSearch (github.com/gitlab.com only): bytecode interpreter written in C++ "faster than CPython" OR "faster than Python" benchmark fibonacci README -> MoonLite-Br/Cpy; README, docs/internals.md and tests/compare_python.sh opened via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: newLISP Neo
baseline: CPython 3.14.4 and CPython 3.12.3 (also original newLISP 10.7.6 tree-walker, the project it derives from)
workload: Recursive fib(30), a 1-million-iteration loop (while and tail-recursive forms), and deep tail-recursion tests; wall time in ms for the newLISP Neo script versus the equivalent bench.py.
claimed_speedup: fib(30): newLISP Neo 42.6 ms vs CPython 3.14.4 86.0 ms (2.02x faster), CPython 3.12.3 186.9 ms, original newLISP 592.5 ms (13.9x faster than original); 1M-iteration while loop 31.3 ms vs CPython 3.14.4 37.2 ms (1.19x faster); tail-recursive 1M loop 17.3 ms (2.15x faster than CPython 3.14.4's while loop); 100M-step self-tail-recursion runs in 1,023 ms where CPython raises RecursionError.
compiler_and_flags: Build needs GCC/MinGW-w64 or Clang with computed-goto support; optimisation flags used for the timings are not stated
tradeoffs: Direct-threaded bytecode VM with automatic fallback to the classic tree-walking evaluator for dynamic-binding and metaprogramming code; generational GC with a 64 MB nursery; keeps the newLISP language (Lisp-like, not Python) and its GPL-3.0 licence; README says all 396 primitives pass the qa-dot suite.
caveats: First-party micro-benchmarks (fib, a counting loop, tail calls) on one unnamed Windows machine; the Python side is one hand-written bench.py per test; CPython 3.14.4 is the interpreter build without a JIT, and the tail-recursion rows compare against a CPython failure, not a time. Small young repository (earliest visible commit 2024-10-19). Forks irr/newlisp-spark and irr/newlisp-neo-fork (aarch64 support) exist and were not opened.
found_via: WebSearch (github.com/gitlab.com only): bytecode interpreter written in C++ "faster than CPython" OR "faster than Python" benchmark fibonacci README -> kimtg/newlisp-neo; README opened via raw.githubusercontent.com and github.com

name: Janet
workload: No benchmark: the README FAQ ('How fast is it?') gives a qualitative comparison only.
claimed_speedup: No numbers. README FAQ: programs 'tend to be a bit faster than they would be in a language like Python' because slow object-oriented abstraction and late-binding lookups are discouraged, while the VM is 'about the same speed as most interpreted languages without a JIT compiler'; it ends with 'YMMV'.
stars_or_usage: 4.4k stars; single-file amalgamation (janet.c + janet.h) for embedding in C and C++
tradeoffs: Lisp-like language with its own syntax, a stop-the-world GC, boxed 8-byte values; threads have isolated heaps; PEG engine built in.
caveats: Hedged, no-number claim kept as the single tier-D record of this run because the project is notable; the same FAQ tells users to write tight critical loops in C or C++, and no Janet-versus-CPython timings were opened, so the claim is unverified.
